. Some metals, such as iron and nickel, are magnetic. Other metals, such as copper and aluminum, are nonmagnetic. Most nonmetals are also nonmagnetic.

. Magnetic forces can act at a distance. In fact, some large magnets can attract magnetic objects from several feet away.

contents.text: Any current-carrying wire that generates a magnetic field is an electromagnet. The wire's shape determines the magnetic field's shape, and the current's direction determines the field's direction.

In the doorbell circuit Emilia and Riley are examining, a straight wire connects the coil of wire to the power source. The current flowing through the wire generates a magnetic field that forms concentric circles around the wire. If the current were to flow in the opposite direction, the magnetic field's shape would stay the same, but its direction would reverse.

textContent.text: In a solid, the particles are held together tightly, and they do not move around freely. Because the particles stay in about the same place, a solid generally keeps a certain shape.
Even though particles in a solid cannot move past one another, they are not completely still. The particles are constantly vibrating, or moving back and forth, in place.

lessons.name: How does particle motion affect gas pressure?

alternativeText.text: A model of the random particle motion in a sample of gas. An arrow from each particle shows the direction of its motion. Some particles bounce from the container walls.

textContent.text: All substances are made up of small particles of matter that are constantly moving. In a gas, these particles can move freely and tend to be far from one another. In fact, the space a gas takes up is mostly empty!

Gas particles move quickly and randomly. They travel in straight lines, changing direction whenever they collide with each other or with the walls of their container. Even though there is a lot of space between particles in a gas, collisions occur frequently because the particles are moving so fast.

Gas particles move quickly and randomly. They travel in straight lines, changing direction whenever they collide with each other or with the walls of their container. textContent.text: All substances are made up of small particles of matter that are constantly moving. In a gas, these particles can move freely and tend to be far from one another. In fact, the space a gas takes up is mostly empty!

Gas particles move quickly and randomly. They travel in straight lines, changing direction whenever they collide with each other or with the walls of their container. Even though there is a lot of space between particles in a gas, collisions occur frequently because the particles are moving so fast.
